title: Window Treatment Stores
one_liner: Specialty window treatment stores sell custom and ready-made blinds, shades, shutters, curtains and draperies, with growth tied to remodeling, housing turnover and premium in-home consultation.
overview: Window treatment stores are specialty retailers focused on indoor and outdoor window coverings, including vertical and horizontal blinds, woven blinds and shades, shutters, curtains, draperies and related installation services. The baseline IBIS report placed 2021 revenue at $1.767 billion, profit at $65 million and profit margin at 3.7%, with 1,923 establishments, 1,669 enterprises and 7,322 employees. Since then, the channel has faced a mixed market: broader US window coverings demand is still supported by energy efficiency, home decor and smart-home adoption, but specialty stores are exposed to soft housing turnover, slower remodeling growth, e-commerce substitution and price competition from The Home Depot, Lowe's, IKEA, Amazon, Blinds.com and other online sellers. A 2024 Kentley report snippet put 2023 Window Treatment Stores revenue at $1.6 billion and 1,508 companies, indicating that specialty-store revenue remained below the 2021 IBIS level even as the broader US window coverings product market continued to expand.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated specialty-store revenue: about $1.6 billion; broader US window covering product market: $4.12 billion projected for 2026 by Fortune Business Insights
key_stats.growth: 2025 estimated specialty-store growth: roughly flat to low-single-digit; adjacent US furniture and home furnishings retail sales rose in early 2025 but turned negative by late 2025 and were -3.4% year over year in April 2026
key_stats.profit_margin: 2021 baseline EBIT margin: 3.7%; 2026 baseline forecast margin: 3.8%
key_stats.employment: 2021 baseline employment: 7,322 workers; 2026 baseline forecast employment: 7,606 workers
key_stats.ecommerce_pressure: Q1 2026 US retail e-commerce share: 16.9% of total retail sales, up from 16.0% in Q1 2025
key_stats.homeownership: Q2 2026 US homeownership rate: 65.2% seasonally adjusted, unchanged from Q2 2025
key_stats.housing_starts: June 2026 US housing starts: 1.427 million SAAR, up 3.5% from June 2025; June 2026 permits: 1.367 million SAAR, down 2.3% from June 2025
key_stats.remodeling_outlook: July 2026 JCHS LIRA forecast: remodeling and repair spending growth slows to 0.5% year over year by Q2 2027, with spending projected at $519 billion through mid-2027

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 estimated revenue: about $1.78 billion, extrapolated from the 2021 IBIS revenue of $1.767 billion and its 2021-2027 projected CAGR of 0.83%
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 estimated growth: about +0.8% versus 2021 under the baseline IBIS forecast
baseline_2022.context: The 2021 baseline expected slow recovery after 2020's -10.5% COVID decline and 2021's +7.0% rebound, with continued pressure from big-box and online competitors.

how_it_makes_money: Stores earn revenue from selling ready-made and custom blinds, shades, shutters, curtains, draperies and related accessories, plus measurement, delivery, installation, repair and in-home design consultation. Higher-margin tickets come from custom sizes, premium fabrics, woven woods, shutters, blackout and cellular shades, motorized systems and whole-home projects where service and fit matter more than commodity price.

cost_structure.purchases: Largest cost category; fabric, vinyl, wood, faux wood, metal, motors, tracks, hardware and vendor-supplied custom products typically absorb the majority of sales dollars.
cost_structure.wages: Labor is material because stores need design consultants, sales staff, measurers, installers and customer service; 2021 baseline wages were $325 million.
cost_structure.rent_and_occupancy: Showrooms carry rent, utilities, display systems, samples and local storage costs, although shop-at-home and franchise models lower fixed occupancy needs.
cost_structure.marketing: Local search, paid ads, direct mail, promotions, designer referrals, franchise fees and review management are increasingly important as consumers start projects online.
cost_structure.freight_and_installation: Bulky custom products create delivery, returns, damage, remake and installer scheduling costs.
cost_structure.profit: 2021 baseline profit was $65 million, equal to a 3.7% EBIT margin; 2026 baseline forecast margin was 3.8%.

current_dynamics: The specialty channel is being squeezed from both sides. Value buyers can source stock blinds and basic shades from big-box and online retailers, while premium buyers still pay for design help, exact measurement, professional installation and custom materials. Demand is less robust than the broader product market because housing turnover is low, remodeling growth is slowing and consumer confidence remains weak: The Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index was 90.8 in July 2026, down 1.4 points from June 2026. Operators with mobile consultation, local SEO, financing, fast quoting and motorized/cordless offerings are better positioned than small showroom-only sellers.
whats_growing: Motorized and smart shades integrated with mobile apps, voice assistants and home automation
Cordless and inaccessible-cord products driven by US safety rules and consumer preference
Cellular, blackout, solar and reflective shades marketed around comfort, privacy and energy efficiency
Shop-at-home consultations, professional measurement and installation services
Eco-friendly materials, recycled fabrics, bamboo, woven woods and low-VOC textiles
Online lead generation and hybrid showroom-plus-ecommerce models
whats_shrinking: Commodity stock blinds sold through independent specialty stores
Catalog-first selling and showroom-only retail models with weak digital lead capture
Free-hanging corded products because 2024 US safety-standard changes pushed the market toward cordless or inaccessible-cord designs
Small independents without installer capacity, financing options or strong local search visibility
Discretionary decorative refreshes tied to weak consumer sentiment and slower remodeling growth
recent_developments: 2024-06-01: Revised ANSI/WCMA A100.1-2022 window-covering safety standard took effect for products manufactured on or after June 1, 2024, pushing most US products toward cordless or inaccessible-cord designs.
2025-04-05: US reciprocal tariff rules began applying to imported goods, including Vietnam-made cordless PVC mini blinds in a 2025 CBP ruling, raising sourcing and landed-cost scrutiny.
2025-09: The Home Depot highlighted recycled-material and energy-saving window treatment products through Blinds.com, reinforcing big-box pressure on specialty stores.
2026-05-18: Census reported Q1 2026 e-commerce sales at $326.7 billion and 16.9% of total retail sales, up from 16.0% in Q1 2025.
2026-07-17: Census reported June 2026 housing starts at 1.427 million SAAR and permits at 1.367 million SAAR, a mixed signal for new-window demand.
2026-07-23: Harvard JCHS forecast remodeling and repair spending growth slowing to 0.5% year over year by Q2 2027, limiting near-term specialty-store tailwinds.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is stable but not high-growth for specialty stores. The broader US product market is expanding on smart-home, energy-efficiency and design trends, but the store-channel opportunity is constrained by e-commerce, big-box pricing and a cooling remodeling cycle. Revenue is likely to stay near the $1.6 billion specialty-store range in 2025-2026, with modest upside for operators that convert online searches into in-home consultations and sell premium custom packages. Margin improvement will be difficult because tariffs, freight, remake risk and advertising costs offset higher average tickets from motorization and custom work.
one_sentence: The US Window Treatment Stores industry remains a small, mature specialty retail channel, competing against big-box, online and manufacturer-direct sellers while defending share through custom measurement, installation, design advice, cordless safety compliance and motorized/smart shade upgrades.

title: Wine & Spirits Wholesaling in the US
one_liner: Wine and spirits wholesalers remain protected by state alcohol distribution rules, but 2025-2026 demand is softer as wine volumes fall, core spirits slow and RTDs take share.
overview: Wine and spirits wholesaling is the middle tier between suppliers and licensed sellers. The 2022 IBISWorld baseline put industry revenue at $129.7 billion after 2.5% growth in 2022, but public 2025-2026 indicators show a flatter, more pressured market: IBISWorld/MarketResearch.com reported $130.4 billion in 2023 revenue, while the broader BLS NAICS 4248 beer, wine and distilled alcohol wholesaler output proxy was $153.25 billion in 2025, down 0.5% from 2024. The structural support is still strong because most states require retailers and on-premise accounts to buy through licensed wholesalers, but the operating story has shifted from post-pandemic reopening and premiumization to inventory discipline, SKU rationalization, value-seeking consumers and growth in spirits-based ready-to-drink cocktails.

key_stats.market_size: $130.4 billion revenue in 2023 for US wine and spirits wholesaling, per the public IBISWorld/MarketResearch.com listing; broader BLS NAICS 4248 beer, wine and distilled alcoholic beverage merchant wholesaler output was $153.25 billion in 2025, down from $153.94 billion in 2024.
key_stats.growth: IBISWorld/MarketResearch.com reported 1.0% annualized revenue growth over the five years to 2023; the 2025 BLS NAICS 4248 proxy declined 0.5% year over year, and WSWA SipSource reported wine and spirits volume declines across 2025.
key_stats.profitability: IBISWorld baseline profit was $4.54 billion in 2022, equal to a 3.5% margin in 2022.
key_stats.employment: IBISWorld baseline employment was 95,527 workers in 2022; the 2022 forecast expected 105,653 workers by 2027.
key_stats.structure: The top three operators accounted for an estimated 33.6% of 2022 industry revenue in the baseline, while 2026 public distributor lists continue to identify Southern Glazer's, RNDC and Breakthru as the leading national wine and spirits distributors.

baseline_2022.growth: 2.5% revenue growth in 2022 and 3.7% annualized growth over 2017-2022.

how_it_makes_money: Wholesalers earn gross margin by purchasing bottles and cases from wineries, distilleries, importers and brand owners, then selling them at wholesale prices to licensed liquor stores, grocery chains, restaurants, bars, hotels, casinos and event operators. Larger distributors also monetize supplier relationships through brand-building, trade marketing, category management, data services, logistics scale, credit terms and digital ordering platforms.
cost_structure: The 2022 cost base was dominated by product purchases and inventory carrying costs, with wages of $8.97 billion equal to about 6.9% of 2022 revenue and profit of $4.54 billion equal to 3.5% of 2022 revenue. Other important 2025-2026 costs include warehouse labor, delivery fleets, fuel, insurance, state compliance, sales commissions, trade promotion, digital ordering systems and working capital tied up in slower-moving wine and premium spirits inventory.

current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is contracting in volume but not uniformly in dollars. WSWA SipSource reported severe 2024 year-end pressure, 2025 second-half softness and continued 2026 contraction across core wine and spirits, with on-premise trends generally outperforming off-premise retail. Distributor economics are being shaped by lower case movement, supplier portfolio resets, tighter inventories, fewer SKUs, consumer trade-down, gas and labor cost pressure, and continued demand for data-rich sales execution. Spirits retain a larger share of beverage alcohol dollars than beer in 2025, but supplier sales declined in 2025, so wholesalers are relying more on mix, service, exclusive books and RTDs than broad category volume growth.
whats_growing: Spirits-based RTDs: DISCUS reported premixed cocktails including spirits RTDs reached $3.8 billion in 2025, up 16.4% year over year.
On-premise relative performance: WSWA reported in May 2026 that bars and restaurants were outperforming retail channels for both spirits and wine.

Digital wholesale ordering: Southern Glazer's and large peers continue investing in B2B platforms, with 2025-2026 distributor competition increasingly tied to account data, forecasting and inventory tools.

Premium and craft niches with strong brands: premiumization is no longer broad-based, but high-end spirits, local craft labels and differentiated wine portfolios still support margin where consumer demand is resilient.
whats_shrinking: Core wine volume: WSWA reported wine depletions down 7.2% in 2024 year-end data, and 2026 updates continued to show negative wine trends.
Core spirits dollars: DISCUS reported US spirits supplier sales of $36.4 billion in 2025, down 2.2% from 2024.
Export-dependent US wine and spirits flows: Wine Institute reported US wine exports to Canada down 78% in 2025, while DISCUS reported US spirits exports down 3.8% in 2025.

Slow-moving SKUs and distributor inventory: 2025-2026 commentary from WSWA and public producer filings points to tighter portfolio management, reduced distributor inventory and heavier discounting in weak wine categories.
recent_developments: 2025-02-24: WSWA SipSource said 2024 year-end data showed spirits depletions down 3.7% and wine depletions down 7.2%.
2025-05-30: Brown-Forman announced a US distributor reshuffle effective 2025-08-01, making Breakthru its largest national distributor partner across 14 US and Canadian markets.
2026-02-05: DISCUS reported US spirits supplier sales of $36.4 billion in 2025, down 2.2%, while spirits RTDs grew 16.4% to $3.8 billion.
2026-03-31: DISCUS reported US spirits exports fell 3.8% in 2025 to $2.37 billion amid trade friction and Canadian shelf removals.
2026-05-21: WSWA SipSource Q1 2026 data showed continued contraction in core spirits and wine, while spirits-based RTDs rose about 30% in off-premise dollars.
2026-06-30: WSWA said May 2026 rolling twelve-month depletion trends remained negative but steadier, with on-premise channels outperforming off-premise.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is cautious rather than collapsing. State distribution laws still give wholesalers durable relevance, and large distributors should keep gaining share through scale, supplier exclusivity, analytics and multi-state coverage. Growth is likely to be uneven: RTDs, strong spirits brands, local craft labels and on-premise accounts can grow, while traditional wine, lower-priority SKUs and over-inventoried premium segments remain pressured. If consumer confidence improves and trade frictions ease after 2026, revenue can stabilize, but near-term case volume is likely to lag revenue because price/mix is doing more work than consumption growth.
themes: State alcohol distribution rules protect the wholesale tier
Volume contraction is replacing broad premiumization as the central challenge
Spirits-based RTDs are the clearest growth pocket in 2025-2026
Distributor consolidation and supplier portfolio resets are intensifying
On-premise channels are healthier than off-premise retail in 2026 updates
Trade friction with Canada and Europe is hurting export-linked suppliers and inventories
Digital ordering, analytics and inventory discipline are becoming core competitive tools

title: Wiring Device Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: US wiring device manufacturers make outlets, switches, connectors, conduit fittings, pole-line hardware and related electrical circuit devices for construction, utilities and industrial equipment markets.
overview: The industry manufactures current-carrying and noncurrent-carrying wiring devices used to wire electrical circuits, including receptacles, switches, wire connectors, electrical boxes, conduit and conduit fittings, pole-line hardware, plugs and cord sets. The 2022 baseline showed $16.0 billion of revenue after 3.4% growth in 2022, with imports of $8.0 billion and exports of $5.2 billion. For 2026, industry revenue is estimated near $16.7 billion, using the 2022 IBISWorld baseline and its 2022-2027 growth path, with upside from data centers, utility transmission and distribution upgrades, and factory automation, but pressure from high import competition, housing volatility and tariff-driven copper and metal cost swings.

key_stats.producer_prices: Current-carrying wiring device PPI was 321.822 in June 2026; noncurrent-carrying wiring device PPI was 580.208 in May 2026
key_stats.construction_indicator: June 2026 housing starts were 1.427 million at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, 3.5% above June 2025
key_stats.construction_spending: June 2026 total construction spending data were published by Census for seasonally adjusted annual-rate categories

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers sell standardized and engineered wiring devices through electrical equipment wholesalers, industrial supply distributors, OEM channels, utilities, contractors and builders. Revenue comes from high-volume current-carrying devices such as receptacles, switches and connectors, plus bulkier noncurrent-carrying products such as conduit, fittings, electrical boxes and pole-line hardware. Large producers also capture value through branded product lines, code-compliant safety features, specification positions with engineers and contractors, and bundled electrical infrastructure offerings for datacenters, factories and utilities.

cost_structure.materials_and_purchases: 2022 purchases were the dominant cost because copper, steel, plastics, resins and fabricated components drive product cost.
cost_structure.wages: 2022 wages were $2.6 billion, equal to about 16.2% of 2022 revenue.
cost_structure.profit: 2022 profit was $866 million, equal to a 5.4% margin.
cost_structure.trade_exposure: 2022 imports were $8.0 billion and 2022 exports were $5.2 billion, making pricing and margins sensitive to exchange rates, tariffs and low-cost production in Mexico and China.
cost_structure.2025_2026_pressure: 2025 copper tariffs and 2026 broader metals tariff changes raised cost and sourcing risk for copper-intensive connectors, electrical components and derivative products.

current_dynamics: In 2025-2026, demand is splitting by end market. Datacenters, utility grid modernization, AI-related power infrastructure and light industrial projects are growing quickly, supporting higher-specification connectors, switches, conduit systems and power distribution accessories. Residential construction remains uneven: June 2026 housing starts were 1.427 million SAAR and 3.5% above June 2025, but permits were 2.3% below June 2025, signaling choppy near-term demand. Producer prices remain elevated: current-carrying wiring devices reached a 321.822 PPI reading in June 2026, while noncurrent-carrying wiring devices reached 580.208 in May 2026. The 2025 copper tariff and 2026 metal-derivative tariff changes add pricing complexity for imported copper-intensive electrical components.
whats_growing: 2025-2026 datacenter electrical infrastructure, including high-specification power distribution, connectors, cabinets and critical power accessories.
2025-2026 utility transmission, distribution and grid resiliency hardware, supported by load growth and aging infrastructure replacement.
2025-2026 light industrial and automation-related wiring devices used in factories, warehouses and process equipment.
2025-2026 energy transition applications, including EV charging, renewables interconnection and building electrification devices.
2026 price realization on metal-intensive products as copper and other electrical-material costs remain high.
whats_shrinking: 2025-2026 commoditized current-carrying devices exposed to low-cost imports and private-label pricing pressure.
2025-2026 residential demand tied to permits, with June 2026 permits 2.3% below June 2025.
2025-2026 office and weaker commercial building applications where post-pandemic space demand remains uneven.
2025-2026 margin flexibility for smaller manufacturers that cannot pass through copper, steel, resin, freight and tariff costs quickly.
2025-2026 China-linked sourcing certainty as tariff regimes and compliance rules change.
recent_developments: July 30, 2025: The White House imposed a 50% tariff on semi-finished copper products and copper-intensive derivative products effective August 1, 2025.
November 7, 2025: Legrand acquired Avtron Power Solutions, expected to generate nearly $350 million of 2025 revenue, and placed it in its Electrical Wiring Systems Division.
February 3, 2026: Hubbell reported 2025 sales of $5.8 billion and 2025 Electrical Solutions sales of $2.17 billion, up 7.1% from 2024.
February 12, 2026: Legrand reported 2025 sales of nearly €9.5 billion, 7.7% organic growth and 16.0% North/Central America organic growth.
April 2, 2026: The White House modified Section 232 metals tariffs so certain aluminum, steel and copper tariffs applied to full customs value beginning April 6, 2026.
July 17, 2026: Census reported June 2026 housing starts of 1.427 million SAAR, up 3.5% from June 2025, while permits were down 2.3% from June 2025.
outlook: Revenue is expected to grow slowly in 2026-2028 rather than break out, with the 2026 market estimated at $16.7 billion and the 2027 market near the prior baseline forecast of $16.9 billion. Upside comes from datacenters, AI power loads, grid hardening, EV charging and industrial automation. Downside comes from rate-sensitive residential construction, import penetration, tariff uncertainty, copper volatility and substitution toward lower-cost imported or standardized devices. Larger branded manufacturers with distributor scale, product breadth and pricing power should outperform smaller operators in 2026-2028.
one_sentence: In 2026, the US Wiring Device Manufacturing industry is a mature roughly $16.7 billion market where datacenters, grid investment and industrial electrification are offsetting softer rate-sensitive residential construction and volatile copper-linked input costs.

title: Women's, Girls' and Infants' Apparel Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: A small, import-squeezed US manufacturing niche where domestic operators survive by designing, jobbing and producing premium, quick-turn or Made-in-USA apparel rather than competing on mass-market price.
overview: This industry manufactures women's, girls' and infants' cut-and-sew apparel from purchased fabric and includes jobbers that design, source materials, arrange production and market finished garments. The 2022 baseline showed a long-term decline caused by offshoring and import penetration, with domestic operators meeting only a small share of US demand. By 2024, industry sales were reported at $3.3 billion, modestly above the depressed 2022 level, but the rebound is narrow: most volume apparel is still imported, while US producers focus on small runs, premium construction, specialty infant products, compliance-sensitive sourcing, private-label development and fast replenishment.

key_stats.apparel_subsector_employment: June 2026 US apparel manufacturing employment: 72,600 jobs
key_stats.apparel_subsector_wages: June 2026 apparel manufacturing average hourly earnings: $23.84
key_stats.apparel_subsector_productivity: 2025 apparel manufacturing output: -6.3%; labor productivity: +4.0%; unit labor costs: +6.0%
key_stats.imports: 2025 US apparel imports: $77.88 billion, down 1.74% from 2024
key_stats.retail_price_signal: June 2026 CPI: women's and girls' apparel +0.1% year over year; infants' and toddlers' apparel -1.4% month over month

baseline_2022.import_penetration: 2022 imports satisfied an estimated 97.0% of domestic demand
baseline_2022.outlook_at_that_time: 2022-2027 forecast revenue CAGR: +1.2%, reaching $3.0 billion in 2027

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes from selling finished women's, girls' and infants' garments, private-label production, contract cut-and-sew work, design and jobber services, sample development, short-run production, premium Made-in-USA lines and specialty products where speed, quality control, compliance or brand value outweigh low-cost offshore sourcing.

cost_structure.materials_and_components: Purchased fabric, trims, notions, thread, labels, packaging and freight are the core variable costs; cotton and synthetic textile prices affect margins.
cost_structure.labor: Cutting, sewing, patternmaking, quality control and production supervision remain labor-intensive; 2026 apparel manufacturing wages averaged $23.84 per hour across the broader subsector.
cost_structure.outsourcing: Many firms use domestic contractors for small runs and overseas vendors for scale production, shifting part of production cost into contracted services and landed cost.
cost_structure.profit: 2022 baseline profit margin was 2.7%, constrained by import competition, retailer pricing pressure and inflation.
cost_structure.overhead: Rent, utilities, compliance, insurance, design staff, sales, marketing, e-commerce operations and inventory financing matter most for smaller domestic operators.
cost_structure.tariffs_and_trade_costs: 2025-2026 tariff changes, customs compliance, forced-labor documentation and sourcing diversification add cost and administrative burden.

major_players: Carter's Inc.
Hanesbrands Inc.
PVH Corp. / Calvin Klein
Tapestry Inc. / Kate Spade
Ralph Lauren Corp.
VF Corp.
Fragmented domestic contractors and jobbers with no dominant industry share
current_dynamics: The industry is being pulled in two directions in 2025-2026. US demand is still overwhelmingly served by imports, with Vietnam, China and Bangladesh among the largest apparel suppliers in 2025, but tariff uncertainty, forced-labor compliance, longer lead times and inventory risk make limited domestic production more valuable for premium, test-and-repeat and compliance-sensitive runs. Domestic producers face higher labor costs and weak pricing power: broader apparel manufacturing output fell 6.3% in 2025 even as labor productivity rose 4.0%, while unit labor costs increased 6.0%.
whats_growing: Premium women's apparel, domestic sample rooms, rapid replenishment, small-batch private label, compliant infant apparel, nearshore/domestic backup sourcing, Made-in-USA branding, digital product development and e-commerce-linked production are gaining relative share.
whats_shrinking: Commodity dresses, blouses, basic girls' apparel, price-sensitive infant basics, large-scale domestic cut-and-sew volume, low-margin contractors without automation or brand relationships, and operators dependent on department-store markdown cycles are losing ground.
recent_developments: 2024: Industry sales were reported at $3.3 billion, with 2021-2024 sales CAGR of 1.1%.
2025: US apparel imports totaled $77.88 billion, down 1.74% from 2024, while import volume fell 3.70%.
2025: Vietnam became the largest 2025 apparel supplier to the US by value, with about $16.7 billion to $17.0 billion in shipments, ahead of China.
2025: Broader US apparel manufacturing output fell 6.3%, hours worked fell 9.9% and unit labor costs rose 6.0%.
April 2025: A US executive order added a 10% baseline tariff on many imports, with additional country-specific duties scheduled from April 9, 2025.
June 2026: BLS reported women's and girls' apparel CPI up 0.1% year over year and overall apparel CPI down 0.9% year over year.
outlook: Through 2026, the industry is likely to remain small and fragmented rather than return to mass domestic production. Sales can hold above the 2022 trough if tariffs, freight uncertainty and compliance risk keep brands using US capacity for speed and risk management, but high wages and inexpensive overseas capacity limit upside. The strongest operators will pair design, sourcing, compliance and quick-turn manufacturing; weak operators exposed to basic apparel will continue to exit or consolidate.

title: Wood Product Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: A fragmented, construction-linked manufacturing niche making miscellaneous wood products, with 2025 demand held back by weak housing but supported by export-oriented wood pellets and higher wood-product pricing in 2026.
overview: The industry sits within manufacturing and covers miscellaneous wood products not classified as sawmills, veneer, engineered wood, millwork, wood containers, manufactured homes or prefabricated buildings. The 2022 IBIS baseline described a mature, low-concentration industry with 2021 revenue of $8.0 billion, 2021 profit of $353 million and 2021 profit margin of 4.4%, with revenue projected to reach $8.2 billion in 2026. Current 2025-2026 public indicators point to mixed conditions: broad NAICS 321 wood product sectoral output was $125.4 billion in 2025, down 0.1% from 2024 in current dollars, while the Federal Reserve's wood product industrial production index rose to 98.734 in 2025 from 97.075 in 2024. Housing remains the core swing factor, with June 2026 housing starts at 1.427 million SAAR, but permits down 2.3% year over year, while wood-product producer prices rose into mid-2026 and wood pellet exports reached 10.09 million metric tons worth $1.93 billion in 2025.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 narrow IBIS-style industry revenue estimate: about $8.3 billion; 2025 broader NAICS 321 wood product manufacturing sectoral output: $125.396 billion.
key_stats.growth: 2025 narrow industry revenue estimate: about +0.5% year over year; 2025 broader NAICS 321 sectoral output: -0.1% year over year; 2025 Federal Reserve wood product industrial production: +1.7% year over year.
key_stats.profit_margin: 2021 baseline profit margin: 4.4%; 2026 baseline forecast profit margin: 4.8%.
key_stats.employment: 2026 June broader NAICS 321 employment: 391,900 employees seasonally adjusted; 2021 narrow baseline employment: 41,780 workers.
key_stats.establishments: 2025 Q4 broader NAICS 321 private establishments: 16,141; 2021 narrow baseline establishments: 7,940.
key_stats.trade: 2025 U.S. wood pellet exports: 10.09 million metric tons valued at $1.93 billion; 2021 narrow baseline exports: $1.535 billion and imports: $4.749 billion.
key_stats.prices: 2026 June BLS wood product manufacturing PPI: 188.275; 2025 December PPI: 179.908.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 baseline estimate: about $8.1 billion in 2021 dollars, inferred from the January 2022 IBIS baseline of $8.0 billion in 2021 and $8.2 billion forecast for 2026.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 baseline growth estimate: about +0.6% year over year, consistent with the January 2022 IBIS forecast CAGR of +0.6% for 2021-2026.
baseline_2022.context: The baseline file was last updated January 2, 2022 and reported 2021 revenue of $8.014 billion, 2021 profit of $353 million, 2021 imports of $4.749 billion, 2021 exports of $1.535 billion and 2021 domestic demand of $11.228 billion.

how_it_makes_money: Operators buy lumber, logs, wood residues, cork, rattan, adhesives and packaging, then manufacture miscellaneous products sold to home builders, home improvement retailers, lumber and building material dealers, wholesalers, commercial users, consumers and export buyers. Revenue comes from product sales across architectural products, wood stock and fuel, home furnishings, containers and pallets, baskets, reels and other specialty wood items, plus contract services such as kiln drying.
cost_structure: Materials are the largest cost category because lumber, wood residues and purchased components drive production economics; the 2022 baseline identified sawmill lumber as the primary input. Labor is meaningful in small-batch and specialty production, with 2025 broader NAICS 321 productivity up 1.2%, hours worked down 1.0% and unit labor costs up 0.3%. Energy, rent, depreciation, freight, packaging, maintenance and compliance costs make up the rest. Profitability is sensitive to lumber price swings because fragmented producers cannot always pass through input inflation quickly; the baseline profit margin was 4.4% in 2021 and forecast at 4.8% in 2026.
major_players: Fragmented industry structure: the 2022 baseline characterized market share concentration as low, with no dominant national player identified.
Enviva LLC: major industrial wood pellet producer; emerged from Chapter 11 on December 6, 2024 and began production at its Epes, Alabama plant in September 2025.
Louisville Ladder Inc.: listed among top NAICS 321999 businesses and relevant to wood ladder products.
California Cedar Products Co.: listed among top NAICS 321999 businesses and relevant to specialty wood products.
American Wood Fibers Inc.: listed among top NAICS 321999 businesses and relevant to wood fiber and fuel products.
current_dynamics: Demand is uneven in 2025-2026. New residential construction is still rate-sensitive, and June 2026 building permits were 2.3% below June 2025, limiting demand for architectural and home-related wood products. At the same time, June 2026 starts rebounded to 1.427 million SAAR and repair/remodel activity supports smaller consumer and building-material categories. Producer prices moved up in early 2026, helped by lumber supply constraints and tariffs, which can lift nominal revenue but pressure margins for firms buying lumber. Export-oriented biomass remains a bright spot, with 2025 wood pellet export volume up slightly from 2024 and export value rising to $1.93 billion.
whats_growing: Wood pellets and wood fuel are growing fastest, with 2025 U.S. wood pellet exports at 10.09 million metric tons and $1.93 billion. Specialty wood stock, kiln drying and products tied to repair/remodel demand are supported by homeowners staying put in a high-rate housing market. Broader wood product real output improved in 2025, with the Federal Reserve annual industrial production index rising 1.7% from 2024. Producer pricing improved in 2026, with the BLS wood product manufacturing PPI reaching 188.275 in June 2026.
whats_shrinking: Housing-linked products remain exposed to weak affordability and soft permitting; June 2026 permits were 3.0% below May 2026 and 2.3% below June 2025. Broad NAICS 321 current-dollar sectoral output slipped from $125.539 billion in 2024 to $125.396 billion in 2025. Employment in broader NAICS 321 has softened from a 2023 annual index of 106.543 to 102.565 in 2025, and low-margin commodity or easily substituted wood items continue to lose share to plastic, metal and imported alternatives.
recent_developments: 2026-07-17: Census reported June 2026 housing starts at 1.427 million SAAR, 3.5% above June 2025, while permits were 2.3% below June 2025.
2026-07-22: BLS reported June 2026 broader NAICS 321 employment of 391,900 and wood product manufacturing PPI of 188.275.
2026-06-29: BLS/FRED published 2025 broader NAICS 321 sectoral output of $125.396 billion, down 0.1% from 2024.
2026-02-19: USDA/FAS data showed 2025 U.S. wood pellet exports of 10.09 million metric tons valued at $1.93 billion.
2025-09-01: Enviva's Epes, Alabama wood pellet plant began production and employed more than 100 full-time workers.
2025-08-08: Commerce announced final countervailing duty rates of 12.12% to 16.82% for Canadian softwood lumber reviewed for 2023 entries.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is flat to modestly positive in nominal terms but uneven by product. Higher prices and export demand for wood fuel support revenue, while weak affordability and soft permits cap housing-linked volume. Operators with diversified end markets, export exposure, efficient lumber procurement and automated finishing/kiln capacity should outperform. Smaller firms remain vulnerable to volatile lumber prices, labor availability, freight costs, import competition and substitution by plastics or metal. A reasonable 2026 narrow-industry revenue range is $8.2 billion to $8.5 billion, compared with the 2022 baseline forecast of $8.2 billion for 2026.
data_year: 2026, using latest public indicators available through June-July 2026 and 2025 annual data where 2026 annual data is not yet available.
one_sentence: Wood Product Manufacturing in the US produces miscellaneous wood products such as kiln-dried lumber, wood stock and fuel, architectural items, home furnishings, ladders, handles, reels, baskets and toothpicks, with revenue tied closely to residential construction, consumer goods demand, lumber costs and export markets for biomass fuel.
